blocks.text: It was now late in the afternoon, and sunset was not far away. We had to accept that our plan was over and could no longer work. With very sad hearts, we agreed with the Professor when he said:

“Let us go back to Madam Mina—poor, poor dear Madam Mina. Everything we can do right now is done. There, at least, we can protect her. But we do not need to lose all hope. There is only one more box of earth, and we must try to find it. When that is done, everything may still be well.” I could see that he spoke as bravely as he could to comfort Harker. The poor man was completely broken in spirit. From time to time, he gave a low groan that he could not hold back. He was thinking of his wife.

With sad hearts, we came back to my house. There we found Mrs. Harker waiting for us. She had an outward look of cheerfulness, which showed how brave and unselfish she truly was. When she saw our faces, her own face became as pale as death. For a second or two, her eyes were closed as if she were saying a secret prayer. Then she said cheerfully:

“I can never thank you all enough. Oh, my poor darling!” As she spoke, she took her husband’s grey head in her hands and kissed it. “Lay your poor head here and rest it. Everything will still be well, dear! God will protect us if that is His will, in His good purpose.” The poor man groaned. His misery was so extreme and deep that there was no place for words in it.

We had a kind of quick supper together. We ate it only as a routine duty, without real interest. Still, I think it cheered us all up a little. Perhaps it was simply the bodily warmth of food for hungry people, as none of us had eaten anything since breakfast. Or the feeling of being together may have helped us. In any case, we were all less miserable, and we saw the next day as not completely without hope. Keeping our promise, we told Mrs. Harker everything that had happened. At times she turned as white as snow when danger had seemed to threaten her husband. At other times she turned red when his deep love and loyalty to her became clear. Even so, she listened bravely and calmly. When we came to the part where Harker had rushed at the Count without caring about the danger, she held tightly onto her husband’s arm. She held it tight, as if holding onto him like that could protect him from any harm that might come. However, she said nothing until the whole story was told and everything had been explained right up to the present time. Then, without letting go of her husband’s hand, she stood up among us and spoke. Oh, how I wish I could give any idea of that scene! There stood that sweet, sweet, good, good woman, shining with the bright beauty of her youth and lively energy. She had the red scar on her forehead. She was aware of it, and we ground our teeth as we looked at it, remembering where it came from and how it got there. There was her loving kindness set against our dark, hard hate. There was her gentle faith set against all our fears and doubts. And there we were, knowing that as far as symbols showed, she—with all her goodness, purity, and faith—was cut off and shut out from God.

“Jonathan,” she said. The word sounded like music on her lips because it was so full of love and gentleness. “Jonathan dear, and all of you, my true, true friends, I want you to keep something in mind through all this terrible time. I know that you must fight, and that you must destroy. You must do this just as you destroyed the false Lucy, so that the true Lucy might live in the life after death. Still, it is not a work of hate. That poor soul who has caused all this misery is the saddest case of all. Just think how great his joy will be when the worse part of him is destroyed too, so that his better part may have never-ending spiritual life. You must feel pity for him too, even though it must not hold back your hands from destroying him.”

As she spoke, I could see her husband’s face grow dark and his features pull tight together. It was as if the fierce feeling inside him were drying up and shrinking his whole self to its deepest part. Without thinking, he held his wife’s hand tighter, until his knuckles looked white. She did not pull back from the pain that I knew she must have felt. Instead, she looked at him, begging with her eyes more strongly than ever. As she stopped speaking, he jumped to his feet. He almost tore his hand away from hers as he spoke:
